lines.narration: Twinkie spells it out: that is Yakuza, actual mafia. Sean hears the word and treats it as a dare.

DK comes through the crowd and stops with his face an inch from Sean's. Nobody moves. He takes a cut of every engine in this room, and he has just been called a monkey's son in front of all of them. Two words settle it. Let's race.
The crowd wants to know with what, his skateboard, and that should be the end of it. Then a voice from the back of the room says take mine.

That is Han, who runs his own crew out of this garage, and he has just handed a kid he has never met a car he built from the block up — for no reason he will explain, beyond wanting to see what Sean can do. Keep an eye on Han. He is the most interesting person in this film.

In the lift Twinkie asks whether he even knows what DK stands for. Sean guesses Donkey Kong. It is Drift King — not a nickname his friends stuck him with, a job title, and nobody in Tokyo races against it for fun.
Twinkie's valuation of the car he is about to be handed is that it is the Mona Lisa of drift work. He sells trainers out of a backpack, so of course it is the Mona Lisa.

Sean drops into the seat. The complete drift education he gets before racing the Drift King lasts about thirty seconds, and it is two moves: rip the e-brake so the back end comes loose, then get on the power and hold it there. That is the whole curriculum. He has never drifted in his life, and he is about to try it in someone else's hand-built car, in front of a few hundred people, against the best driver in the city.
Before the start DK pulls Neela into him in front of everyone, holds it, and lets the whole garage watch. That is not affection. That is inventory.
Sean looks across at the harness and the helmet and grins at him. He has no idea what he is doing, and the grin is the only thing he brought.
Up on the other levels, the crowd is watching it relayed on each other's phones. Whatever happens in the next two minutes, everyone in Tokyo who matters knows by morning.

Then he gets greedy on a corner, the back end goes further than he meant it to, and Han's car lays a line of sparks down the concrete. Twenty seconds in, he has already damaged the one thing he was lent.
DK takes the identical corner broadside and makes it look like the corner was built for him. That contrast is the only thing this race is about.
DK has the spiral to himself now and takes it sideways the whole way down.
In all that noise two people are not cheering: Twinkie, and Neela beside him, watching the exit with nothing on their faces at all.

Sean comes out dead last, the front of Han's car torn open and smoking. The barrier breaks and the crowd swarms him. He has lost in front of four hundred people who all know exactly what that repair bill is.
Han comes to the window of his own ruined car and does not raise his voice. Sean has been in Tokyo barely a week, and he already owes a stranger an entire car.
He gets home after midnight and finds Lieutenant Boswell, his father, sitting in the dark with a beer, waiting up.
Boswell is on his feet now. Have you been racing, Sean.
Sean's answer is to lift a car key off the desk and head for the door.

In the back room his father lays out exactly where he stands. There is nowhere else left to send him. If this does not work out here, he goes to jail — live under this roof by these rules, or get out. Sean has heard this speech in every town they ever lived in. This is the first one with a cell at the end of it.
Yes, sir. That is all he gives him, and he gives it from the doorway.
Sean tells him he will get him his money. Han asks why he is talking like he has a choice. Sean does not set the terms of anything anymore.
Han explains the arrangement on the drive: a debtor is holding out on him, and Sean is the one going in to collect. Sean does not ask one question about what collecting means.
The place turns out to be a bathhouse, and the debtor is a mountain with a wolf inked across his whole back, soaking in the pool. Sean walks in wearing a towel.
He stands over him and keeps pressing anyway. The debtor stops answering, stands up out of the water, and turns out to be a foot taller than the kid doing the asking.
He gets up, goes straight back in, and comes straight back out, one shoe short. Han sent a seventeen-year-old to lean on a man twice his size, and got the result he expected.
The orange car runs the expressway at dusk with the whole city going the other way.

On the night drive they make the actual deal. Sean is in the pick-up and delivery business now. Han might call once a week or once an hour. He does not care if Sean is sick as a dog or in bed with Beyonce — he calls, Sean shows. Only if you teach me to drift, Sean says. Han tells him this is not a negotiation. Sean tells him he wasn't negotiating.
